{{Short description|Concept in graph theory and network analysis}}

{{Network Science}}
In [[graph theory]] and [[network theory|network analysis]], '''group centrality''' generalizes the concept of [[centrality]] to sets of [[vertex (graph theory)|nodes]] in a network. Introduced by Everett and Borgatti in 1999, group centrality measures are intended to lift the restriction of usual centrality measures only applying to individual nodes.
For instance, the analysis of the centrality or marginalization of certain groups in the network of an organization can be enabled by group centrality measures.<ref name="10.1080/0022250X.1999.9990219">{{cite journal | vauthors = Everett MG, Borgatti SP | title = The centrality of groups and classes | journal = The Journal of Mathematical Sociology | volume = 23 | issue = 3 | pages = 181–201 | year = 1999 | doi = 10.1080/0022250X.1999.9990219 | bibcode = 1999JMSo...23..181E }}</ref>

One complication when searching for groups of a given size <math display="inline">k</math> with maximum group centrality arises from the fact that for many measures, this problem is [[NP-hard]].<ref name="angriman2020group">{{cite conference | vauthors = Angriman E, van der Grinten A, Bojchevski A, Zügner D, Günnemann S, Meyerhenke H |title = Group centrality maximization for large-scale graphs | book-title = 2020 Proceedings of the Twenty-Second Workshop on Algorithm Engineering and Experiments (ALENEX) | pages = 56–69 | year = 2020 | publisher = SIAM | arxiv=1910.13874}}</ref> Therefore, [[heuristics]] and [[Approximation_algorithm|approximation algorithms]] are typically used in practical applications.<ref name="10.1002/net.22248">{{cite journal | vauthors = Camur MC, Vogiatzis C | title = A survey on optimization studies of group centrality metrics | journal = Networks | volume = 84 | issue = 4 | pages = 491–508 | year = 2024 | doi = 10.1002/net.22248 | url = https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/net.22248 }}</ref>

[[File:Group Centrality Example.svg|thumb|upright=1.75|Groups with maximum group degree centrality (left), group closeness (middle), and group betweenness (right) marked in red, for <math display="inline">k=3</math>.]]

==Group degree centrality==
In analogy to the conceptually simple '''degree centrality''', which measures the [[degree (graph theory)|degree]] of a node, the '''group degree centrality''' of a group <math display="inline">S</math> of nodes is simply defined as the number of non-group nodes adjacent to nodes in <math display="inline">S</math>. Formally, the group degree centrality <math display="inline">C_D(S)</math> of a group <math display="inline">S \subseteq V</math> of a given graph <math display="inline">G = (V,E)</math> is defined as
:<math>C_D(S)= \left |\bigcup_{v \in S} N(v)\setminus S \right |</math>

When the size <math display="inline">k</math> is part of the input, the problem of determining a set <math display="inline">S</math> of size <math display="inline">k</math> with maximum group degree centrality is NP-hard.<ref name="10.3390/math8101810">{{cite journal | vauthors = Krnc M, Škrekovski R | title = Group degree centrality and centralization in networks | journal = Mathematics | volume = 8 | issue = 10 | pages = 1810 | year = 2020 | doi = 10.3390/math8101810 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Group closeness centrality==
In a [[Connected component (graph theory)|connected]] [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]], the [[Normalization (statistics)|normalized]] '''group closeness centrality''' (or '''group closeness''') of a group is the reciprocal of the average length of the [[Shortest path problem|shortest path]] between the group and all other nodes in the graph. More precisely, the group closeness centrality <math display="inline">C(S)</math> of a group <math display="inline">S \subseteq V</math> in a connected graph <math display="inline">G=(V,E)</math> is defined as
:<math>C(S)= \frac{|V|-|S|}{\sum_{v \in V} \text{dist}(v,S)}</math>,
where
:<math>\text{dist}(v,S) := \min_{u \in S} \text{dist}(v, u)</math>
denotes the distance of <math display="inline">v</math> to <math display="inline">S</math>, that is, the distance to the closest node in <math display="inline">S</math>. Hence, just like [[Closeness centrality]], this measure can be regarded as the normalized variant of the reciprocal of a '''farness''' measure, which for the group case is given as 
<math display="inline">f(S) = \sum_{v \in V} \text{dist}(v,S)</math>.

The problem of finding a group <math display="inline">S</math> of given size <math display="inline">k</math> with maximum group closeness is NP-hard.<ref name="10.1007/978-3-319-46922-5_4">{{cite conference | vauthors = Chen C, Wang W, Wang X | title = Efficient Maximum Closeness Centrality Group Identification | book-title = Databases Theory and Applications. ADC 2016 | volume = 9877 | pages = 43–55 | year = 2016 | publisher = Springer | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-46922-5_4 }}</ref>

==Group betweenness centrality==
'''Group betweenness centrality''' is the generalization of [[betweenness centrality]] and similarly quantifies the number of times group nodes act as a bridge along the shortest path between two other nodes. Formally, for a graph <math display="inline">G=(V,E)</math> it is defined as 
:<math>C_B(S)= \sum_{s \neq v \neq t \in V}\frac{\sigma_{st}(S)}{\sigma_{st}}</math>
where <math display="inline">\sigma_{st}</math> is the total number of <math display="inline">s</math>-<math display="inline">t</math> paths and <math display="inline">\sigma_{st}(S)</math> is the number of <math display="inline">s</math>-<math display="inline">t</math> paths passing through <math display="inline">S</math>.
Analagously to individual betweenness, group betweenness may be normalized by dividing through the number of pairs of nodes not including the group <math display="inline">S</math>, which for [[directed graph|directed graphs]] is <math display="inline">(n-|S|)(n-|S|-1)</math> and for undirected graphs is <math display="inline">\frac{1}{2}(n-|S|)(n-|S|-1)</math>, where <math display="inline">n = |V|</math>.

Finding the group <math display="inline">S</math> of a given size <math display="inline">k</math>
with maximum group betweenness is NP-hard.<ref name="puzis2007finding">{{cite journal | vauthors = Puzis R, Elovici Y, Dolev S |url=https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.5555/1365534.1365539| title = Finding the most prominent group in complex networks | journal = AI Communications | volume = 20 | issue = 4 | pages = 287–296 | year = 2007 | publisher = SAGE Publications }}</ref>

==Group current flow closeness centrality==
'''Group current flow closeness centrality''' generalizes current flow closeness of individual nodes. Unlike conventional (group) closeness, current flow closeness not only considers the length, but also the number of shortest paths by treating the graph as a resistor network and considering current flow in this network, rather than shortest paths. Let <math display="inline">G=(V,E)</math> be a graph (representing a resistor network with edge resistances) and <math display="inline">S \subseteq V</math>. Then formally, group current flow closeness is defined as
:<math>C_{CF}(S)= \frac{n}{\sum_{u \in V} v_{uS}(u)}</math>,
where <math display="inline">v_{uS}(u)</math> is the voltage of <math display="inline">u</math> when a unit current enters <math display="inline">G</math> at <math display="inline">u</math> and leaves it at <math display="inline">S</math>.<ref name="10.1145/3308558.3313490">{{cite conference | vauthors = Li H, Peng R, Shan L, Yi Y, Zhang Z | title = Current Flow Group Closeness Centrality for Complex Networks? | book-title = The World Wide Web Conference | series = WWW '19 | pages = 961–971 | year = 2019 | publisher = Association for Computing Machinery | doi = 10.1145/3308558.3313490 | url = https://doi.org/10.1145/3308558.3313490 | arxiv = 1802.02556 }}</ref>

The maximization problem is NP-hard.<ref name="10.1145/3308558.3313490">{{cite conference | vauthors = Li H, Peng R, Shan L, Yi Y, Zhang Z | title = Current Flow Group Closeness Centrality for Complex Networks? | book-title = The World Wide Web Conference | series = WWW '19 | pages = 961–971 | year = 2019 | publisher = Association for Computing Machinery | doi = 10.1145/3308558.3313490 | url = https://doi.org/10.1145/3308558.3313490 | arxiv = 1802.02556 }}</ref>

==Other group centrality measures==
* Group eigenvector centrality
* Group harmonic centrality
* GED-Walk centrality

==Algorithms==

[[File:Group centrality greedy algorithm example.gif|upright=0.8|thumb|Result of the greedy algorithm on the [[Tutte_graph| Tutte graph]] for <math> k = 1,...,5</math> for group degree centrality (top), group closeness (middle), and group betweenness (bottom). Note how the result of the greedy algorithm for any <math>k</math> is a subset of the solution for <math>k+1</math>. Since the Tutte graph is [[regular_graph|regular]], every 2-independent set, i.e., a set where nodes are at least distance three apart, is a maximum degree centrality group.]]

For many group centrality measures, the problem of finding a group of a given size with maximum centrality can be formulated as an [[integer linear program]].<ref name="10.1080/10556788.2016.1167892">{{cite journal | vauthors = Veremyev A, Prokopyev O, Pasiliao E | title = Finding groups with maximum betweenness centrality | journal = Optimization Methods and Software | volume = 32 | pages = 369–399 | year = 2017 | doi = 10.1080/10556788.2016.1167892 | url = https://doi.org/10.1080/10556788.2016.1167892 | url-access = subscription }}</ref><ref name="10.1137/1.9781611975055.18">{{cite conference | vauthors = Bergamini E, Gonser T, Meyerhenke H | title = Scaling up Group Closeness Maximization | book-title = 2018 Proceedings of the Meeting on Algorithm Engineering and Experiments (ALENEX) | pages = 209–222 | year = 2018 | publisher = Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics | doi = 10.1137/1.9781611975055.18 | url = https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/1.9781611975055.18 }}</ref>
For example, consider the following integer linear program for group degree centrality maximization:
:<math> \begin{align}
      \text{max} & \quad \sum_{v \in V} y_v \\
\text{s. t.} &\quad
      \sum_{v \in V} x_v = k\\
     & \forall v \in V: \begin{cases}
x_v+y_v \leq 1 \\
y_v \leq \sum_{u \in N(v)} x_u \\
x_v,y_v \in \{0,1\}
\end{cases}
\end{align}</math>
Here, the <math>x_v</math> variables indicate whether <math>v</math> is in the group, while the <math>y_v</math> variables indicate if <math>v</math> is a non-group neighbor. Thus, the objective function corresponds to <math>C_D(S) = |N(S) \setminus S|</math>, where <math>S = \{v \in V \mid x_v = 1\}</math>. This objective is maximized under the constraint <math display="inline">|S| = \sum_{v \in V} x_v = k</math>, as required.


Since it is NP-hard for many group centrality measures to find a subset 
<math display="inline">S \subseteq V</math> of the vertices of a graph <math display="inline">G=(V,E)</math> with <math display="inline">|S| = k</math> that maximizes the centrality of <math display="inline">S</math>, numerous [[heuristics]] and [[Approximation_algorithm|approximation algorithms]] have been proposed. One widely used [[greedy algorithm]]
can be expressed as follows in [[pseudocode]].

<syntaxhighlight lang="d" line>
 function greedy(G : graph, k : positive integer):
     S ← {}
     while |S| < k do:
          v ← vertex maximizing centrality of S ∪ {v}
          S ← S ∪ {v}
     return S
</syntaxhighlight>
Note how the vertex chosen in line 4 is not necessarily uniquely determined, and therefore neither is the result of the greedy algorithm.

For non-negative [[monotonic function|monotone]] [[submodular set function|submodular set functions]], such as GED-Walk centrality, this greedy algorithm is already guaranteed to yield a <math>(1-1/e)</math>-approximation. For other measures like group closeness, which do not satisfy submodularity, this algorithm can still be a useful heuristic.<ref name="10.1137/1.9781611975055.18">{{cite conference | vauthors = Bergamini E, Gonser T, Meyerhenke H | title = Scaling up Group Closeness Maximization | book-title = 2018 Proceedings of the Meeting on Algorithm Engineering and Experiments (ALENEX) | pages = 209–222 | year = 2018 | publisher = Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics | doi = 10.1137/1.9781611975055.18 | url = https://epubs.siam.org/doi/abs/10.1137/1.9781611975055.18 }}</ref>

===Implementations===
The software library [[NetworkX]] supports the evaluation of group degree centrality, group closeness and group betweenness, as well as obtaining the most prominent group with respect to group betweenness centrality.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://networkx.org/documentation/stable/reference/algorithms/centrality.html#group-centrality |title=Centrality — NetworkX documentation: Group Centrality |author=NetworkX Developers |website=NetworkX |access-date=2026-07-28}}</ref> 

The network analysis toolkit [[NetworKit]] supports the evaluation and maximization of group degree centrality, group closeness, group harmonic centrality, group betweenness and more.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://networkit.github.io/dev-docs/python_api/centrality.html#networkit.centrality.ApproxGroupBetweenness |title=networkit.centrality — NetworKit documentation |author=NetworKit Developers |website=NetworKit |access-date=2026-07-28}}</ref>
